# Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting

###### Abstract

Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with
frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal
system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call
_recursive self-improvement_ (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an
environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and
naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution.
Here we introduce EvoForesight, a sustainable evolution agent system
grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously
interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by
internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these
interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a
recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each
prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction
adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live
environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from
the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the
FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world
outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked
first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a
195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked
among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest
baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley–Terry points. More broadly, these results
suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as
an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended
environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on
fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own
experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that
growth. Our resources are available at
[https://github.com/RUCAIBox/EvoForesight](https://github.com/RUCAIBox/EvoForesight).

## 1 Introduction

Intelligence is often measured by what a system can do at a single
moment in time \[[19](#bib.bib11), [2](#bib.bib12)\]. Yet the more
consequential question may not be how capable a model is today, but
whether it can become more capable through its own experience
\[[23](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14)\]. Across the
natural and social sciences, the systems we regard as most powerful
(e.g., biological evolution, the scientific method, human expertise) are
precisely those that improve themselves cumulatively, correcting past
errors and compounding past gains \[[21](#bib.bib15), [8](#bib.bib16),
[25](#bib.bib17)\]. This suggests that an ideal artificial system should
be measured less by what it can do at any single moment than by how its
capabilities form and grow over time. A system that improves itself from
experience is a prerequisite for AI that acts as an autonomous agent and
as a genuine instrument of discovery. In this work, we study this form
of _recursive self-improvement_ (RSI) in the concrete and demanding
setting of real-world event forecasting.

Studying recursive self-improvement, however, is not merely a matter of
method. It places unusually high demands on the research setting itself.
An agent can only improve recursively if its environment keeps posing
fresh challenges and can tell, without human intervention, whether the
agent is doing better than before. What this calls for is an interactive
environment, yet the fixed datasets that dominate today’s evaluation
offer no such thing: inert and unchanging, they neither renew the
challenge nor judge progress on their own. Real-world event forecasting,
we argue, is a natural testbed for such study: it is _grounded_ in the
unfolding world rather than a hand-constructed dataset, _verifiable_
through future events whose objective ground truth arrives with time,
and _non-stationary_ because the world keeps changing. Together these
properties close the loop that recursion requires: the agent observes
the world, makes predictions, receives future outcomes, learns from the
resulting experience, and improves the predictions it makes next (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")a).
Whereas prior work on event and time-series forecasting
\[[30](#bib.bib25), [11](#bib.bib26)\] has largely pursued single-shot
predictive accuracy, we instead treat forecasting as an environment in
which to study how agents improve recursively through continuous
interaction with a changing world.

Succeeding in this environment first requires a few foundational
capabilities for solving any single forecasting task. An agent must be
able to _gather_ task-relevant evidence from a vast information space,
as exemplified by search-augmented systems \[[26](#bib.bib3),
[27](#bib.bib5)\], and to _reason_, combining and weighing that evidence
to draw multi-step conclusions \[[5](#bib.bib6), [1](#bib.bib10)\]. Both
capabilities are already standard in existing systems, and we treat them
as the foundation on which our self-improvement mechanisms build.
Recursive self-improvement goes further, requiring a capability
different in kind: an agent that not only solves the task in front of it
but also changes its own behavior in light of past successes and
failures. Such an agent addresses a distinct question: how its capacity
to solve tasks can itself keep improving. We take this ability to
_evolve_ as the central concern of this work, and reserve the name
EvoForesight for the framework we propose to realize it (Section
[4](#S4 "4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).

Realizing such an evolving agent runs against a basic limitation of
today’s AI: it is largely static and dependent on outside intervention
to advance, a set of parameters frozen at release rather than a system
that keeps improving on its own \[[25](#bib.bib17), [4](#bib.bib18)\].
This shows up on two fronts. Evaluation is static, scoring a model on a
fixed dataset \[[6](#bib.bib1), [16](#bib.bib2)\] that can be memorized
or contaminated; and improvement is passive, with capability gains
driven from outside by human-curated data and offline retraining
\[[12](#bib.bib19), [7](#bib.bib20)\] rather than by the model’s own
experience. This condition also differs from neighboring lines of work:
self-training on self-generated data \[[28](#bib.bib21),
[13](#bib.bib22)\] lacks an external, verifiable ground truth and can
reinforce a model’s own biases; continual learning \[[15](#bib.bib23),
[20](#bib.bib24)\] operates over static or artificially partitioned task
streams rather than real, non-stationary feedback; and reinforcement
learning for reasoning \[[23](#bib.bib8), [22](#bib.bib9)\] optimizes
reward on a task but does not, by itself, target improvement that
compounds across time. By _recursive_, we mean exactly this compounding:
the parameters, skills, and environment produced by one round of
improvement become the input to the next, forming a self-improvement
loop rather than a one-off gain \[[21](#bib.bib15), [8](#bib.bib16)\].

Our central argument departs from most work on self-improvement, which
pushes on a single lever, be it the model’s weights
\[[13](#bib.bib22)\], its prompts \[[10](#bib.bib29)\], or its memory
\[[24](#bib.bib30)\]. What makes self-improvement _sustainable_, we
argue, is a system that keeps accumulating experience on its own rather
than being fed hand-curated data from outside, and our answer is a
_living environment_ in which the agent continually acts, observes
outcomes, and learns. The logic is directional. The environment is the
source, posing progressively harder tasks that supply the experience
without which no further improvement is possible; the agent’s
_parameters_ and _skills_ are the two forms its evolution takes, both
shaped from one substrate, the forecasting _trajectories_ that are
reinforced into parameters, distilled into skills, and mined for the
weaknesses that build a harder environment. The three thus couple into a
single self-sustaining loop, in which the environment evolves to let the
agent keep evolving.

Building on this view, we introduce EvoForesight, an event-forecasting
framework for studying recursive self-improvement in a continuously
evolving real-world environment, in which the agent and its environment
co-evolve. EvoForesight comprises three modules arranged as a closed
loop rather than a pipeline. Prometheus, a _living data environment_,
continually ingests real-world events to form the non-stationary,
verifiable world in which forecasting takes place. Branchus, an _agentic
forecaster_, produces predictions together with their full trajectories,
generating the learning substrate described above. Athena, the
_recursive-evolution engine_, learns from these trajectories through
reinforcement learning and skill accumulation to drive self-improvement.
The loop closes when Athena’s improvements strengthen Branchus’s
forecasts, and these stronger forecasts in turn place new demands on
Prometheus, pushing the environment to evolve and sustaining an
open-ended cycle of agent-environment co-evolution.

This co-evolution produces a strong forecasting system. Across all four
LLMs, Branchus ranks among the top three overall and leads its block,
and because every result is scored against real-world outcomes, this
consistency reflects an advantage intrinsic to the design (BT of
$`62.2`$ on Qwen3.8-Max, $`+10.7`$ over the strongest baseline in Table
[1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
More importantly, the gains compound rather than saturate: as the
agent’s own live trajectories accumulate into a growing pool, the skills
distilled from them lift forecasting quality round by round rather than
jumping once and plateauing (Figure
[6](#S2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Our experiments trace this improvement to how environment, parameters,
and skills evolve together, each by its own means. Reinforcement
learning sharpens the _parameters_, tightening probabilistic judgment
beyond what accuracy registers (the numeric calibration score improves
by $`0.31`$–$`0.38`$ while choice accuracy moves by only $`1.3`$ points
in Figure
[5](#S2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
yet its reach is bounded by the experience available. The experience
distilled into _skills_ lifts capability without touching the weights,
learning from only limited trajectories rather than repeated rollouts
and so sidestepping the instability that gradient updates can introduce.
The _environment_ closes the loop: when it co-evolves with the agent,
synthesizing verifiable tasks aimed at the agent’s demonstrated
weaknesses, these otherwise isolated and bounded gains add up to a
larger improvement (Figure
[9](#S2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
This is evidence that recursive self-improvement arises from the three
levers evolving as one.

Taken together, these findings establish recursive self-improvement as
the co-evolution of an agent and its living environment. The environment
is the abstraction we commit to. Our first contribution is to construct
a _real, dynamic, and verifiable_ environment for forecasting: grounded
in the unfolding world, non-stationary as that world changes, and scored
against outcomes that resolve on their own. This environment lets all
three levers improve in concert. Its verifiable outcomes become rewards
that sharpen _parameters_; its live experience supplies the trajectories
that distil into _skills_; and its dynamic form lets it be rewritten
toward the agent’s exposed weaknesses, so each round feeds the next. Our
second contribution turns this opening into method: EvoForesight
formalizes the environment, the agent, and the recursive-evolution
engine as three modules in a closed loop (Section
[4](#S4 "4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
More broadly, the development of AI may shift from training static
models on fixed datasets toward cultivating evolving agents within
living environments, and with it the measure of progress: the rate,
ceiling, and durability of a system’s improvement, which only an
evolving environment can reveal.

Forecasting is the concrete setting we build and study, and the way we
construct this environment, and the methodology that evolves an agent
inside it, carry over to any setting that is grounded, verifiable, and
non-stationary, so the same loop can be extended to far more general
scenarios. It also recasts how recursive self-improvement might be
pursued, suggesting that progress may come less from any single,
ever-larger model than from co-evolving parameters, skills, and the
environment that supplies their experience. Such progress is not without
cost: it remains bounded by the quality and quantity of available
experience, long-horizon evaluation is expensive, and stability under
non-stationary drift is not guaranteed. Yet even bounded, it reframes
the question with which we began. The deepest measure of intelligence
may lie less in what a system can do at a single moment than in whether
it can grow stronger from its own experience, and our study offers
concrete evidence that such growth can be made to occur, and to be
measured, in a real and verifiable world.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/deepevolve_overview.png)

Figure 1: Overview of EvoForesight for recursive self-improvement in
real-world event forecasting. a, The closed loop connects question
generation, forecasting, and evolution, with resolved outcomes supplying
verifiable rewards and updates feeding into subsequent rounds. b,
Prometheus generates questions through templates and agent-driven
discovery, followed by temporal validation, deduplication, conflict
detection, and diversity-aware selection. c, Branchus separates evidence
gathering, by a _search team_ of a scheduler, searcher, and critic, from
probabilistic prediction, by a _predict team_. The search team is
time-sensitive, as its result depends on when it runs, while the predict
team is time-invariant, reasoning only over the search team’s cached
evidence and reasoning trajectories. Both teams retrieve relevant
forecasting skills. d, Athena updates the predict team’s parameters
using cached evidence and verifiable rewards, distills search
trajectories into reusable forecasting skills, and converts observed
weaknesses into task-synthesis skills for Prometheus. Resolved outcomes
inform parameter and environment updates but are withheld from the
behavior-level judge.

## 2 Results

### 2.1 Experimental Design and EvoForesight Framework

To forecast future events and to test whether an agent can improve
itself from doing so, we develop EvoForesight, a framework that turns
experience into capability through a closed loop of three components.
Prometheus, the living data environment, gathers daily news and
synthesizes it into forecasting tasks whose ground truth is revealed
only once the events resolve. Branchus, the agentic forecaster, gathers
evidence with external tools and estimates the probability of each
event, producing a full prediction trajectory. Athena, the
recursive-evolution engine, consumes these trajectories and drives
improvement along three axes. It applies reinforcement learning with
verifiable rewards (RLVR) to update the parameters of Branchus, distills
trajectories into reusable forecasting skills, and evolves adversarial
task-synthesis skills in Prometheus to make the environment harder. Each
forecasting trajectory is rich enough to feed all three axes at once:
because a future-event prediction forces the agent to gather evidence
and weigh it under uncertainty, the same trajectory can be reinforced
against its resolved outcome, mined for reusable skills, and analysed
for the weaknesses from which a harder environment is built. Experience
is thus fed back to improve the agent’s parameters, its skills, and its
environment jointly, realizing the recursive self-improvement loop at
the heart of this work. The subsections that follow examine these three
axes in turn, after first establishing the strength of the system as a
whole.

We draw forecasting tasks from two complementary sources. The first is
FutureX \[[29](#bib.bib27)\], an external benchmark refreshed every week
that asks models to predict events in the coming week. Its tasks span
four difficulty levels (L1 to L4), take multiple-choice, ranking, and
numerical forms, and cover domains from finance and politics to sports,
natural disasters, and technology, so strong performance reflects
general forecasting ability. The second is a higher-throughput
evaluation synthesized by Prometheus, used purely as a task generator
with its adversarial evolution disabled so the evaluation stays
unbiased. Both sources are genuinely live rather than static or cached.
Each day, Prometheus ingests fresh news from $`125`$ websites and writes
forecasting questions about events that resolve the following day, so
Branchus must predict outcomes whose ground truth does not yet exist.
This one-day horizon shortens the verification cycle and lets us
evaluate models far more frequently than a weekly benchmark allows.

Every question concerns a future event, so predictions are verified
against realized outcomes rather than a fixed answer key. For the
Prometheus evaluation, once an event resolves we task Codex
\[[17](#bib.bib4)\] with retrieving the realized outcome from the open
web and scoring the prediction against it. Beyond raw accuracy, we
report a _calibration_ metric: the model outputs a probability for each
event, and we check whether the empirical frequency of those events
matches the predicted probabilities. We also stabilize these
per-question scores before aggregating. On FutureX we adopt its official
sliding-window Bradley–Terry (BT) model \[[3](#bib.bib28)\], which
infers a consistent latent strength from head-to-head weekly results. On
Prometheus, a single day of questions is too small and too variable to
rank harnesses reliably, so unless stated otherwise every reported
number averages over several consecutive days of live evaluation.

starting point. We pair the evolved system with four LLMs that differ in
size, provider, and reasoning behavior (Qwen3.8-Max, GPT-5.6-Sol,
DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Claude-Opus-4.6) and compare against a diverse
suite of baselines on the Prometheus-synthesized evaluation (Table
[1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting");
Section
[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Models and Implementation ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
for details), with FutureX giving the externally refreshed view below
(Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Regardless of the base model, EvoForesight is strongest: it attains the
highest BT score and best rank in every block, and the four Branchus
configurations occupy the top three positions overall, led by
Qwen3.8-Max at a BT of $`62.2`$. The margin over the best baseline
ranges from $`+10.7`$ to $`+0.5`$ BT but never changes sign. Because the
evaluation resolves against real-world outcomes rather than a fixed
answer key, this cross-model consistency indicates an advantage
intrinsic to EvoForesight rather than a fortunate match between one
design and one model. The subsections that follow isolate how each axis
of self-improvement turns the agent’s own experience into this frontier.

Model capability and agent design are complementary rather than
substitutable. A stronger LLM lifts the ceiling for every system, so the
strongest result in the table is reached by placing Branchus on the most
capable model (Qwen3.8-Max); conversely, Branchus rescues a weaker base,
reaching rank $`3`$ on DeepSeek-V4-Pro and outscoring every baseline
irrespective of the model those baselines are built on. The two effects
compose and neither alone is sufficient to reach the frontier, which
suggests that further gains require jointly improving the base model and
the agent that scaffolds it, motivating the recursive-evolution
mechanisms studied in the remainder of this paper.

Crucially, this advantage reflects well-calibrated judgement rather than
over-confident guessing. Raw accuracy alone does not separate the
systems: on choice questions the baselines occasionally edge out
Branchus by a few tenths of a point, for example MAS on DeepSeek-V4-Pro
and OpenClaw on Claude-Opus-4.6. The decisive gap instead appears on
calibration and numeric sharpness: Branchus attains the best Brier score
in three of the four blocks and the best relative WIS on both
Qwen3.8-Max ($`0.737`$) and GPT-5.6-Sol ($`0.865`$), so its interval
forecasts are tighter than the strongest baseline rather than merely
competitive. Because the Brier score and WIS jointly penalize
over-confident wrong answers and unjustified hedging, Branchus does not
trade calibration for accuracy; its probabilities and intervals
faithfully reflect the evidence it gathered, which is what lifts it to
the top of the BT ranking even where its top-$`1`$ accuracy is only
matched.

Finally, this advantage is stable over time rather than an artifact of a
single evaluation window. Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
tracks the sliding-window BT rating of every harness across four
consecutive weekly evaluations, and Branchus (dark blue) sits at or near
the top of the field in each panel, holding its lead as the task
distribution is refreshed, whereas standard workflows are both lower and
less steady, swinging more sharply between weeks and gaining less from a
stronger LLM. We attribute this gap to two related bottlenecks: these
workflows execute fixed, largely one-pass evidence gathering, so
additional model capability is spent re-reading the same limited context
rather than expanding source coverage; and they lack an explicit
mechanism for tracking hypotheses and calibrating confidence across
steps, so long chains of reasoning accumulate uncorrected errors and
drift toward over-confident predictions. Together, these limitations
explain why standard workflows saturate well below the frontier defined
by Branchus, and why simply scaling up the LLM is insufficient to close
the gap on long-horizon forecasting tasks. This frontier is where our
agent begins rather than ends: the remaining subsections show that
recursively evolving Branchus pushes it beyond this already-leading base
form, so that capability grows from the agent’s own experience over
successive rounds instead of jumping once and plateauing.

LLMs on one axis of forecasting quality, with every axis oriented so
that upward movement is an improvement. Fine-tuning on successful
trajectories lifts every axis, and the improvement is led by calibration
rather than raw accuracy. Left: choice accuracy. Right: numeric interval
forecasts, measured by relative WIS.

((a)) Qwen3-4B-Thinking.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/rlvr_qwen3_8b.jpg)

((b)) Qwen3-8B.

Figure 5: RLVR sharpens both forecasting-quality metrics across LLMs.
For each LLM, we compare the base model against its RLVR-tuned
counterpart on choice accuracy (left blue axis) and the numeric score
(right red axis, $`1-\mathrm{bWIS}`$). Each metric shows two
side-by-side bars, the base model and its RLVR-tuned counterpart, as

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_performance_mape.jpg)

((a)) MAPE across evolution rounds.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_performance_brier.jpg)

((b)) Brier score across evolution rounds.

Figure 6: Evolving skills improve forecasting quality continuously.
Distilled skills, inserted at inference without touching the weights,
sharpen Branchus’s forecasts on both axes of forecasting quality.
Because each round adds its live trajectories to the pool (nested pools
of $`88`$, $`186`$, and $`262`$ trajectories), the skills Athena
extracts over successive evolution rounds lift forecasting quality round
by round rather than in a one-off gain. Left: numeric accuracy, measured
by MAPE. Right: calibration, measured by the Brier score. _For both
metrics, lower is better._

The first of the three axes is the model’s parameters. The obstacle to
internalizing forecasting experience is that the environment is live and
easily contaminated: once an event resolves, its answer becomes
retrievable from the web, so the task can no longer train a model to
predict rather than look up. The clean window is short, yet RFT and RLVR
must roll out and refine over the same tasks repeatedly, which leaves
too little uncontaminated, verifiable experience to support training at
all. The _function-oriented_ design of Branchus removes this obstacle by
splitting the incompatible needs across teams organized by function: a
time-sensitive search team gathers evidence while a question is still
open, and a time-insensitive predict team reasons over it into a
forecast. We cache the evidence and both teams’ trajectories while the
task is still fresh, so the many RFT/RLVR rounds that follow read from
this frozen pool rather than from a web that has since revealed the
answer. Because the predict team is trained only on fixed, pre-cached
evidence, it cannot influence what it sees, which also closes the
on-policy shortcut in which RLVR would manufacture answer-entailing
evidence; any gain reflects better reasoning over the same information.
Once enough cached trajectories resolve into verifiable labels, we train
the predict team with two complementary paradigms: RLVR optimizes
against each resolved outcome, and RFT fine-tunes on successful
trajectories.

Under this function-oriented protocol, RLVR yields consistent gains
across both LLMs (Figure
[5](#S2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")):
choice accuracy rises by $`1.3`$ points on each model, while the numeric
score ($`1-\mathrm{bWIS}`$) improves by $`0.31`$ and $`0.38`$. These
clean, consistent gains from a reward computed against resolved outcomes
are themselves evidence that the design has kept contamination out of
the training signal, since a leaked answer would have collapsed the
reward long before it could sharpen the model. The two kinds of metric
respond at different rates, and we attribute this to the metrics
themselves. Accuracy is binary and insensitive to how belief mass
shifts, whereas calibration is continuous and reflects any move toward
the true outcome probabilities. Calibration thus surfaces improvements
too subtle for accuracy to register, acting as an early indicator that
RLVR is tightening the model’s probabilistic judgment even when the
top-1 answer is unchanged.

RFT, under the same protocol, also improves every axis across two LLMs,
again led by calibration (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")):
accuracy rises by $`0.7`$ to $`2.9`$ points, while Brier and relative
WIS improve consistently. These gains compound over rounds rather than
being spent in one pass: training GLM-4.7-Flash with RFT on each round’s
cached trajectories, the first round already sharpens forecasts (Brier
$`0.651\!\to\!0.636`$, relative WIS $`1.02\!\to\!0.99`$), and the second
round keeps pushing them down (Brier $`0.630`$, relative WIS $`0.98`$)
as the task pool grows from $`600`$ to $`1000`$ (Figure
[3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
This is the multi-round self-improvement at work: because the
environment is live, every round brings a fresh batch of newly resolved
events, and the new experience distilled from them carries the
forecasting quality a step further. The live stream of information is
thus what sustains continual evolution, so the model never runs out of
fresh, verifiable experience to learn from. Evolving the environment
alongside the model amplifies this effect, since tasks that keep
targeting the agent’s current weaknesses turn this incoming information
into richer experience for the next round and drive still larger gains,
which we discuss in Sec.
[2.7](#S2.SS7 "2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting").

### 2.4 Evolving skills unlock recursive self-improvement from fleeting live trajectories

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_count.jpg)

((a)) Number of distilled skills.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_coverage.jpg)

((b)) Topical coverage.

Figure 7: Distilled skills scale across evolution rounds. As the
collected trajectories grow round by round, Athena keeps distilling new
skills from them, so the library expands rather than saturating, and
later skills extend into domains seen only rarely before. Left: the
number of distilled skills at each evolution round. Right: the breadth
of topical coverage, measured by the number of the domains and concrete
tasks that the skills cover.

The live trajectories that the function-oriented design cached for RLVR
can instead be read for the lessons they contain, internalizing the same
scarce experience in a lighter, more transparent form: reusable
forecasting _skills_ that sit outside the model weights and are invoked
at inference time. A single live trajectory thus feeds more than one
lever, as RLVR turns it into a parameter update while skill distillation
turns the same record into an explicit, inspectable procedure learned
without any gradient update. The stakes here are sharper than for
parameters, because fresh trajectories are collected only within each
task’s short open window, so the axis is useful only if a mere handful
of them can already lift the system. We let Athena distill the lessons
from Branchus’s trajectories into skill entries and build libraries over
three evolution rounds, from nested pools of $`88`$, $`186`$ and $`262`$
live trajectories, each round extending the previous one as it
accumulates more trajectories, giving Branchus the current library at
inference so that any change in performance is attributable to the
skills alone.

A handful of live trajectories already unlocks clear improvements on
both axes of forecasting quality (Figure
[6](#S2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Relative to the skill-free Branchus baseline, the Brier score drops from
$`0.135`$ to $`0.122`$ ($`0.013`$ lower), and the same pattern reappears
on the numeric side of the benchmark, where the MAPE falls from
$`2.80\%`$ to $`2.28\%`$ ($`0.52`$ points lower). Two features of the
result are worth emphasising. First, the skills are inserted without
touching the model weights, so the gain is a direct measurement of the
value of externalised live experience rather than an interaction with
the underlying policy. Second, the joint improvement in the Brier score
and the numeric MAPE mirrors the pattern observed under RLVR, indicating
that distilled skills and reinforcement learning act along the same axis
of forecasting competence and can, in principle, be composed.

As each round accumulates more live trajectories into the growing pool,
forecasting quality improves round by round, though at a slowing pace.
Each pool adds gain on top of the last, with the Brier score reaching
$`0.007`$, $`0.012`$ and $`0.013`$ below the baseline across the three
rounds and the MAPE descending from $`2.80\%`$ to $`2.40\%`$, $`2.32\%`$
and $`2.28\%`$ (Figure
[6](#S2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 2.3 Search-prediction decoupling adapts RFT and RLVR to contamination-prone live environments ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
so the skills distilled at a later round help Branchus more than those
from an earlier one. Later rounds move the aggregate metric less but are
far from idle, for what they add is breadth: topical coverage broadens
roughly threefold, from $`168`$ domains and $`173`$ tasks at round $`1`$
($`88`$ trajectories) to $`479`$ domains and $`505`$ tasks at round
$`3`$ ($`262`$ trajectories) (Figure
[7(b)](#S2.F7.sf2 "Figure 7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 2.4 Evolving skills unlock recursive self-improvement from fleeting live trajectories ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
as later skills reach domains that appeared only rarely before. The
slowdown therefore reflects a shift in what each new live trajectory
buys rather than saturation of the mechanism: the dominant forecasting
patterns are captured early, so even a small pool internalizes the core
modes of reasoning, after which added skills extend coverage into
domains the evaluation set rarely samples and their benefit is diluted
in the overall metric. Having now internalized the same trajectories
into both parameters and skills, we next compare where each axis helps
and at what cost, examining how the benefit of skills depends on task
structure, before turning to the environment that supplies the
experience.

### 2.5 Skill evolution guides evidence gathering while parameter evolution sharpens evidence use

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_efficiency.jpg)

((a)) Where skills help, by task structure.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/cost_comparison.jpg)

((b)) What skills cost, by model size.

Figure 8: Skills versus parameter updates: where they help and what they
cost. Externalizing experience into skills and internalizing it into
parameters act at different stages and carry different costs, so the two
axes are complementary rather than interchangeable. Left: forecasting
accuracy and the agent’s tool-call budget as the skill library grows,
separated into structure synthesis problems that reuse recurring
patterns and open synthesis problems from unfamiliar domains. Right: the
compute cost of skill extraction against parameter updates as the base
model scales up.

|                |                                 |       |         |        |         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------- | ----- | ------- | ------ | ------- |
| Stage          | Step                            | Calls | Input   | Output | Total   |
| Evaluation     | Step scoring (searcher, critic) | 6.49  | 100,781 | 8,476  | 109,257 |
|                | Scheduler scoring               | 1.45  | 34,487  | 2,259  | 36,745  |
|                | Trajectory diagnosis            | 1.05  | 52,396  | 1,098  | 53,494  |
| Extraction     | Experience extraction           | 1.02  | 29,363  | 1,372  | 30,735  |
|                | Experience filtering            | 0.91  | 29,520  | 508    | 30,029  |
| Generalization | Four-level generalization       | 2.02  | 18,409  | 2,354  | 20,763  |
