Table 2: Token cost of distilling skills from one trajectory, by stage.
Values are averages per trajectory; output tokens include reasoning
tokens.

The same forecasting experience can be turned into capability in two
ways. Parameter evolution _internalizes_ it, folding the lessons of past
trajectories into the model weights, whereas skill evolution
_externalizes_ it, writing those lessons out as explicit, reusable
procedures that sit beside the weights. The two forms act on different
stages of forecasting: externalized skills shape how the agent
_explores_ for evidence, while internalized parameters shape how well it
_uses_ the evidence it has gathered, and a practical system must know
when each is worth its cost. To expose where skills help, we partition
the questions synthesized by Prometheus by how they were generated:
_structure synthesis problems_, scraped from fixed fields of a
designated website and instantiated over a hand-designed template, so
they share a stereotyped structure and a few recurring reasoning
patterns; and _open synthesis problems_, freely proposed by Codex from
the day’s news, so they are heterogeneous in topic, format, and required
evidence. Alongside accuracy and calibration, we track the agent’s
_tool-call budget_, which reveals whether skills make the agent do more
work per question or the same work more directly.

Where skills help turns out to depend sharply on how the problem was
synthesized (Figure
[8(a)](#S2.F8.sf1 "Figure 8(a) ‣ Figure 8 ‣ 2.5 Skill evolution guides evidence gathering while parameter evolution sharpens evidence use ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
On structure synthesis problems, which reuse a few recurring patterns,
recursively evolved skills cut the agent’s tool use: as the library
grows, tool calls drop by 44% (from $`32`$ to $`18`$ per question) while
MAPE stays at least as strong as the skill-free baseline. One encounter
is often enough for Athena to distil a skill that captures the whole
family, letting Branchus skip exploratory search and act on a compiled
shortcut. On open synthesis problems drawn from domains the skills were
never designed for, the signature reverses: the agent issues 13% more
tool calls (from $`30`$ to $`34`$ per question) and investigates more
broadly, and here the quality gains are the largest in the plot, with
MAPE falling by 32% (from $`3.40\%`$ to $`2.31\%`$) and closing almost
the entire gap to the accuracy on structure synthesis problems. On these
novel problems a skill cannot supply the exact procedure, so it instead
acts as a high-level plan that opens up broader lines of search than the
agent would pursue unaided. Externalizing experience therefore improves
the agent’s _exploration_: it makes evidence gathering either more
direct, when a matching skill compiles the task away, or more
far-reaching, when a loosely related skill widens the search over an
unfamiliar domain.

Internalizing the same experience into parameters acts on a different
stage and leaves this exploration behaviour untouched. Because Athena
updates only the predict team, which reasons over cached evidence, and
never the search team that issues tool calls, RLVR changes neither the
number of searches nor what evidence is gathered; what it changes is how
well that fixed evidence is _used_, as the predict team learns to weigh
and integrate the same observations into a sharper, better-calibrated
forecast. The two forms also differ sharply in cost. Externalization is
pure inference, with no rollout and no backward pass, a gap that only
widens with model size (Figure
[8(b)](#S2.F8.sf2 "Figure 8(b) ‣ Figure 8 ‣ 2.5 Skill evolution guides evidence gathering while parameter evolution sharpens evidence use ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
and Table
[2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2.5 Skill evolution guides evidence gathering while parameter evolution sharpens evidence use ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
This cheapness, however, comes with a ceiling: a few trajectories, on
the order of $`88`$, already yield most of the achievable gain, because
externalization can only reorganise patterns some trajectory already
exhibits and cannot discover strategies outside Branchus’s current
repertoire. Internalization spends its larger budget precisely on
behaviours the model does not yet exhibit, and keeps improving past the
point where externalization plateaus.

Externalization and internalization are therefore complementary rather
than substitutes: externalizing experience into skills gives rapid,
cheap gains in exploration up to a well-defined ceiling, and
internalizing it into parameters gives slower, costlier gains in
evidence use that push beyond it. This suggests a simple division of
labour for the recursive loop, in which a compute-efficient system
externalizes experience into skills every round and reserves parameter
updates for occasional longer bursts, recovering most of the capability
of pure RLVR at a fraction of the compute and letting the same budget
drive many more turns of the agent and environment loop. The compute
saved this way is best spent on the third axis, the environment itself,
since, as we show next, an environment that keeps posing new
weakness-targeted tasks is what decides whether recursive improvement
continues to compound or eventually flattens.

### 2.6 An evolving environment continuously turns the agent’s own failures into adversarial challenges

The two agent-side axes share a common ceiling: whether experience is
internalized into parameters or externalized into skills, both can only
reorganise what the agent has already encountered, so each is bounded by
the distribution of tasks the environment poses, and neither can lift
this ceiling because neither controls the experience it feeds on. The
third axis does. Rather than draw tasks from a fixed distribution, we
let the _environment_ evolve in response to the agent, which is the
engine of the living environment set out in the introduction: the
agent’s own forecasts expose its weaknesses, and those weaknesses drive
the environment to pose harder tasks. We operationalise it by coupling
Athena to the task synthesis of Prometheus: Athena analyses each batch
of trajectories not for what worked but for what failed, distilling each
recurring failure mode into a _task-synthesis skill_ that Prometheus
uses to generate the next round, so that the environment continuously
turns the agent’s own failures into the adversarial challenges it must
next overcome. The forecasting trajectory thus feeds its third and final
lever, the same record reinforced into parameters and distilled into
skills now mined for the failures from which a harder environment is
built, closing the recursive loop in which all three axes evolve from
one shared substrate.

The questions synthesized under the evolved skill are measurably harder
for the current agent, the signature a weakness-targeting environment
should produce. Evaluating the same Branchus checkpoint on questions
from the original and the evolved skill, selection accuracy drops from
$`0.60`$ to $`0.53`$ and the Brier score worsens from $`0.52`$ to
$`0.58`$ (Figure
[9(a)](#S2.F9.sf1 "Figure 9(a) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ 2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
This added difficulty is not noise: if the evolved questions were mere
coin flips, the agent’s confidence would stop separating correct from
incorrect answers, and AUROC would collapse toward $`0.5`$. Instead
AUROC is essentially unchanged, edging up from $`0.678`$ to $`0.68`$, so
the agent’s uncertainty remains informative. By mining the agent’s own
trajectories for its failure modes, the environment manufactures
genuinely harder yet answerable questions, which is the raw material the
next round of self-improvement needs.

A worked example makes concrete what the statistics summarise (Appendix
[E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Prometheus: Skill-Conditioned Question Synthesis ‣ Appendix E Case Study ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Running the synthesis pipeline twice over an identical corpus, once with
the baseline generator and once after injecting a task-synthesis skill
from $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}`$, isolates the skill’s effect while
the source material is held fixed. For a Women’s 77 kg weightlifting
final, the baseline keeps the nearly-decided predicate “who wins the
gold”, whereas the skill-steered generator reframes the same event
around a precise numeric quantity, the gold medallist’s total in
kilograms, with the 268 kg standard as a salient threshold, giving a
question that remains objective and resolvable from one official page
yet is genuinely uncertain. The same sharpening recurs across domains,
as a coarse air-quality category band becomes a request for the exact
index value. These _numerical-forecast_ and _threshold-judgment_
categories are where Branchus’s error is highest, and the skill-steered
batch concentrates its questions there. The environment-level skill thus
holds each question’s objectivity and reproducible resolvability fixed
and moves only its _difficulty_ into the dimension where the agent is
weakest, the mechanism behind the aggregate drop in accuracy and Brier
at preserved AUROC reported above.

### 2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/skill_difficulty.jpg)

((a)) Difficulty of synthesized questions.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/env_coverage.jpg)

((b)) Breadth of distilled experience.

Figure 9: Environment evolution targets genuine weaknesses and enriches
the resulting experience. Coupling task synthesis to the agent’s own
failure modes turns its weaknesses into harder challenges, and the
richer trajectories these produce feed back into the system’s evolution.
Left: the difficulty of the synthesized questions under the original
versus the evolved skill, showing that evolution raises difficulty while
keeping each question well-posed and resolvable. Right: the distilled
experience obtained from the same trajectory pool, comparing a
weakness-targeting environment against a fixed one in the number of
skills and the breadth of their coverage.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/hard_prob_improvement.jpg)

Figure 10: Fine-tuning on the harder, evolved questions pays off. Across
every metric, RFT on the adversarially synthesized hard problems
improves over plain RFT. Each row is drawn on its own scale.

The harder questions are valuable not in themselves but because the
richer experience they generate flows back into both of Branchus’s
evolution axes, so a weakness-targeting environment improves the system
more than a fixed one does. For the skill axis, the evolved questions
probe parts of the task space the agent has not mastered, and the
experience distilled from them covers substantially more ground. From
the same pool of $`262`$ trajectories, coupling task synthesis to the
agent’s weaknesses raises the number of distilled skills from $`1312`$
to $`1403`$ and broadens coverage from $`320`$ to $`337`$ domains and
from $`331`$ to $`357`$ concrete tasks (Figure
[9(b)](#S2.F9.sf2 "Figure 9(b) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ 2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
The gain outlasts the current round, since a skill library spanning more
domains is more likely to match the questions the agent meets next,
making experience accumulated under an evolving environment more broadly
reusable than experience accumulated under a static one.

The parameter axis benefits in the same direction. Relative to plain
RFT, RFT on the adversarially synthesized hard problems improves every
forecasting metric we track, lowering the Brier score by $`1.6\%`$,
raising AUROC by $`2.7\%`$, and tightening numeric forecasts by
$`1.0\%`$ in relative WIS and $`4.0\%`$ in Md-sAPE (Figure
[10](#S2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 2.7 A targeted and challenging environment drives sustained system evolution ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Because both axes draw on the same enriched experience, the evolved
environment lifts the system through the skills it distils and the
parameters it updates alike. The agent and its environment thus enter a
productive cycle: each round of environment evolution exposes a
weakness, and each round of agent evolution repairs it, so capability
compounds rather than saturates. This is our clearest evidence that an
evolving environment is an essential part of recursive self-improvement
rather than an optional add-on, since a fixed distribution of tasks
eventually exhausts what it can teach whereas one that keeps distilling
challenges from the agent’s own mistakes holds the loop open.

Taken together, the preceding subsections trace a single trajectory as
it is turned, in turn, into updated parameters, distilled skills, and a
harder environment. No one of these axes is sufficient on its own:
parameters and skills internalize only the experience already available,
and it is the evolving environment that keeps that experience expanding.
It is their joint evolution, grounded in the information-rich
trajectories that event forecasting naturally produces, that turns a
strong forecaster into one whose capability compounds across rounds,
exactly the form of recursive self-improvement set out in the
introduction.

## 3 Discussion

This study presents EvoForesight, a recursive self-improvement framework
that treats real-world event forecasting as a living environment the
agent learns inside, rather than a static task it is scored against.
Across a diverse suite of agent baselines spanning model families and
domains, EvoForesight attains the strongest forecasting performance,
matching or surpassing every alternative with clear gains in calibration
(Section
[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Beyond this static advantage, the system keeps improving from its own
experience. Skill evolution shows this most clearly: as each round adds
its live trajectories to the pool, the skills distilled from the growing
pool lift forecasting quality step by step rather than in a single jump.
These results show that an evolving agent inside an evolving environment
can sustain improvement where prior approaches saturate, reframing
progress from training a static model on a fixed dataset to cultivating
a system whose capability accrues from its own experience.

The central contribution of EvoForesight is a real, dynamic, and
verifiable environment that turns forecasting into a usable training
signal. This environment couples three modules: a living data source
(Prometheus), an agentic forecaster (Branchus), and a
recursive-evolution engine (Athena). Such an environment is difficult to
train on directly, because forecasting data expires once an event
resolves, and a question answerable only before resolution loses its
training signal afterward. EvoForesight addresses this by separating
evidence gathering from prediction: a time-sensitive search team caches
the evidence available at forecast time, and a time-invariant predict
team learns over that frozen context, so resolved outcomes supply
verifiable rewards while the agent sees only the information available
to it at forecast time. Within this environment the agent retains
experience through two complementary routes, compressing it into
parameters by reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards and
externalizing it into an explicit, reusable skill library distilled from
forecasting trajectories. Combining the two yields the fast, inspectable
gains of skill accumulation together with the deeper gains that only
parameter updates reach, a combination that surpasses any single-lever
training.

These two routes, one internal and one external, strengthen different
capabilities of the agents. Parameter evolution writes experience into
the weights: reinforcement learning trains the predict team on cached
evidence, so the model draws fuller and better-calibrated conclusions
from the information in hand. Skill evolution writes experience into an
explicit, reusable library that guides the search team, so the agent
gathers evidence more accurately and comprehensively in the first place.
The two are complementary rather than redundant: one sharpens reasoning
over fixed evidence, the other improves the evidence that reasoning
receives. Learning along both routes at once is itself a key technical
enabler of recursive self-improvement, because they differ not only in
what they strengthen but in what they demand of the experience that
drives them (Section
[2](#S2 "2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Internal learning needs a large volume of trajectories to evolve stably,
since reinforcement learning must roll out and refine over the same
tasks repeatedly, which makes it hard to apply in a live,
contamination-prone environment whose clean, verifiable window is short.
External learning is far more stable, as a mere handful of live
trajectories already lifts the system within each task’s narrow open
window, exactly the regime in which parameter updates run short of data.
Running both in tandem thus lets the system keep improving from scarce
fresh experience, so the strongest configurations pair a
parameter-trained predict team with a mature skill library, and the
effective capability of the system is defined jointly by its weights and
its accumulated skills.

Both weights and skills draw on one source, the experience the
environment supplies, which makes the environment the governing term of
the system, the one on which the other two depend. A fixed environment
fails this role in two ways. First, it saturates: both routes exhaust
the same task distribution, as the predict team resamples evidence it
has already mastered and the skill library finds only patterns it has
already distilled, so added compute relearns the same regularity and
further agent-side training struggles to drive the curve higher. Second,
it is prone to contamination: once the outcomes of past events become
publicly retrievable, the model can exploit a reasoning shortcut,
recalling a resolved answer instead of reasoning toward a forecast. To
sustain improvement, the environment itself must therefore evolve, and
evolve purposefully: it must stay fresh rather than reuse resolved
events, and it must grow harder in a targeted way, posing new tasks at
the current edge of the agent’s competence. The dynamic environment we
construct meets both demands by drawing new events and scoring them
against outcomes that resolve only in the future, which provides a
signal that cannot have been seen in advance, to force the agent to
genuinely forecast rather than recall and to keep the experience that
drives recursive self-improvement renewing round after round.

This evolution is driven by the cooperation between Athena and
Prometheus. Athena distills the failures it finds in the agent’s
trajectories into task-synthesis skills, and Prometheus uses them to
generate the next round of tasks, so the environment acts as a teacher
whose difficulty tracks the agent’s current weaknesses: as the agent
improves and its weaknesses shift, the tasks shift with them, and both
sides keep changing. Two boundaries constrain this teacher. First, it is
only as discerning as its diagnoses: a wrong prediction is an explicit
failure that can be turned into a harder task, whereas a silent weakness
such as overconfidence stays hidden from this signal, so the environment
improves the agent most where its errors are already visible. Second,
its pace is set by the world, because a round resolves only after the
events it concerns have occurred, so questions that take months to
settle make each round of improvement slow and costly.

Several limitations of the present system point to future directions,
each bearing on how far recursive self-improvement can run. The first
concerns the experience the environment supplies, its fuel: where
resolvable, informative events are rare or strongly culture-dependent,
trajectories stay thin, so broadening the sources of experience in both
quantity and quality is a natural way to raise the ceiling of the
recursive loop. The second concerns the skill library as the world
drifts, since a skill distilled under one regime may apply differently
once the underlying regularity shifts; forgetting, time-weighting, and
failure detection would keep the externalized experience reliable, so
that improvement accumulates genuine capability. The third concerns the
evolution operators themselves: richer forms of parameter evolution that
let updates compound round by round as skill accumulation already does,
and more expressive forms of skill evolution in how experience is
distilled, organized, and retrieved, both offer room to turn the same
trajectories into larger gains. Pursuing these directions together is a
natural way to strengthen the recursive loop.

The lasting product of this work is a methodology, a technical route for
exploring recursive self-improvement, portable to any domain that is
grounded, verifiable, and non-stationary. Carrying it elsewhere asks
only for the three terms forecasting supplies here: a living source of
tasks whose outcomes resolve over time, an agent that records its
trajectories, and an evolution engine that turns those trajectories into
updated weights, reusable skills, and harder tasks. Scientific
discovery, software engineering, and strategic planning each meet this
description. In every such domain the environment commands the process,
as an agent climbs only as far as its environment raises the bar, so
building environments that keep evolving is the central problem
recursive self-improvement must solve. In place of ever larger static
models on ever larger static datasets, the alternative is to cultivate
evolving agents within evolving environments, setting the ceiling on
progress by the openness of the environment rather than the size of a
snapshot. EvoForesight is an early demonstration that this path can be
walked, moving the measure of intelligence from what a system can do at
a single moment to whether it can grow stronger through its own
experience, observably and reproducibly in a real and verifiable world.

## 4 Approach

### 4.1 Overview

EvoForesight is a closed loop in which an agent and its environment
improve one another over time, realized by three modules (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
rather than a feed-forward pipeline from input to prediction. Prometheus
(Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Prometheus: A Living Data Environment ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
the living data environment, turns real-world news into forecasting
tasks whose ground truth is revealed only once the events resolve,
supplying both the tasks and an objective, time-delivered reward.
Branchus (Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Branchus: Agentic Forecasting System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
the agentic forecaster, gathers evidence with external tools and reasons
over it to issue a probabilistic prediction, producing both an answer
and a full _trajectory_. Athena (Section
[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Athena: Recursive Evolution System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
the recursive-evolution engine, converts these trajectories back into
capability: it updates Branchus’s parameters, distills its reasoning
into reusable skills, and analyzes its failures into task-synthesis
skills that make Prometheus pose harder, weakness-targeted questions.
The three thus form a single evolving system, in which a stronger
Branchus meets a steadily more demanding Prometheus, while the world
remains the external ground of every reward.

Notation and Problem Setup. We make this loop precise before
instantiating its three modules. Branchus is a policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$
with parameters $`\theta`$ that, given a forecasting question $`q`$ and
a repository of forecasting skills $`\mathcal{S}`$, produces a
probabilistic prediction together with the reasoning trajectory that
supports it,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(\hat{p},\,\tau)\;\sim\;\pi_{\theta}(\,\cdot\mid q,\,\mathcal{S}\,),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\hat{p}`$ is a distribution over the possible outcomes of $`q`$
and $`\tau`$ records the evidence gathered, the hypotheses entertained,
and the intermediate decisions taken. Prometheus is the environment
$`\mathcal{E}`$: at round $`t`$ it emits a batch of questions
$`\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}`$, and once the underlying events resolve it
reveals, for each $`q`$, an objective outcome $`y_{q}`$ that defines a
verifiable reward

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r(q,\hat{p})\;=\;\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\arg\max_{o}\hat{p}(o)=y_{q}\,\right]\in\{0,1\},
``` |  | (2) |

which checks whether the outcome the model deems most likely matches the
resolved outcome $`y_{q}`$, so that time rather than human annotation
supplies supervision. We summarize the state of the system at round
$`t`$ by the triple

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Sigma^{(t)}\;=\;\big(\theta^{(t)},\,\mathcal{S}^{(t)},\,\mathcal{E}^{(t)}\big),
``` |  | (3) |

whose three components are the agent’s parameters, its accumulated skill
library, and the environment that supplies its tasks. Athena advances
this state through three evolution operators, each learning from the
trajectory pool $`\mathcal{T}^{(t)}=\{\tau\}`$ collected over
$`\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}`$: a parameter update $`\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}`$, a
skill update $`\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}`$, and an environment update
$`\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}`$ (Section
[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Athena: Recursive Evolution System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Writing the rollout of $`\pi_{\theta^{(t)}}`$ on $`\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}`$
as $`\mathcal{T}^{(t)}`$, one round of recursive self-improvement is the
update

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{(t+1)}=\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}\!\big(\theta^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)}\big),\quad\mathcal{S}^{(t+1)}=\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}\!\big(\mathcal{S}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)}\big),\quad\mathcal{E}^{(t+1)}=\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}\!\big(\mathcal{E}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)}\big),
``` |  | (4) |

which maps $`\Sigma^{(t)}\!\mapsto\!\Sigma^{(t+1)}`$ and makes the
products of one round the raw materials of the next (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
The word *recursive* refers to this composition: the triple co-evolves
rather than converging to a fixed set of weights, because
$`\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}`$ keeps generating a next batch
$`\mathcal{Q}^{(t+1)}`$ matched to the capability of the updated agent
$`\pi_{\theta^{(t+1)}}`$.

1: state
$`\Sigma^{(t)}=(\theta^{(t)},\mathcal{S}^{(t)},\mathcal{E}^{(t)})`$,
forecast horizon $`H`$

2: updated state $`\Sigma^{(t+1)}`$

3: $`\triangleright`$ Task synthesis (Prometheus)

4: $`\mathcal{D}^{(t)}\leftarrow\textsc{Crawl}(\mathcal{E}^{(t)})`$

5:   // crawl web pages: calendars, feeds, developing news

6:
$`\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}^{(t)}\leftarrow\textsc{Gen}(\mathcal{D}^{(t)},\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}^{(t)})`$

7:   // synthesize question drafts
$`q=(e,o,f,t_{\mathrm{cut}},t_{\mathrm{dl}})`$

8:
$`\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}\leftarrow\textsc{Select}\circ\textsc{Filter}(\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}^{(t)})`$

9:   // temporal/dedup/conflict filtering, diversity-aware selection

10: $`\triangleright`$ Rollout (Branchus)

11:
$`\mathcal{T}^{(t)}\leftarrow\{\,(\hat{p},\tau)\sim\pi_{\theta^{(t)}}(\cdot\mid q,\mathcal{S}^{(t)}):q\in\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}\,\}`$

12: observe outcomes $`y_{q}`$ and rewards $`r(q,\hat{p})`$ as events
resolve within $`H`$

13: $`\triangleright`$ Evolution (Athena)

14:
$`\theta^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}(\theta^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)})`$

15:   // parameter level: RLVR

16:
$`\mathcal{S}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}(\mathcal{S}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)})`$

17:   // behavior level: skill distillation

18:
$`\mathcal{E}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}(\mathcal{E}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)})`$

19:   // environment level: adversarial synthesis

20: return
$`\Sigma^{(t+1)}=(\theta^{(t+1)},\mathcal{S}^{(t+1)},\mathcal{E}^{(t+1)})`$

Algorithm 1 EvoForesight: one evolution round

### 4.2 Prometheus: A Living Data Environment

Prometheus constructs batches of objective, short-horizon prediction
questions through two complementary mechanisms. In *template-based
generation*, source-specific adapters retrieve public calendars,
schedules, feeds, and structured pages, identify upcoming events, and
instantiate predefined question templates. In *agent-driven open
discovery*, Codex \[[17](#bib.bib4)\] gathers information from relevant
websites, interprets scheduled events and developing stories, and
constructs structured question drafts. Its sources span many domains,
including sports, economics, monetary policy, energy, weather, public
health, technology, government affairs, and cryptocurrency. Candidates
from both routes enter a shared construction and publication pipeline,
which we formalize next. Formally, each candidate question is a tuple

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       q\;=\;\big(e,\,o,\,f,\,t_{\mathrm{cut}},\,t_{\mathrm{dl}}\big),
       ```                                                              |     | (5) |

pairing an identifier $`e`$ for the underlying real-world event with an
identifier $`o`$ for the specific outcome being asked about (such as the
winner of a match or its total score), an answer format $`f`$, a
generation time $`t_{\mathrm{cut}}`$ that marks when the question is
created, and a forecast deadline $`t_{\mathrm{dl}}`$. The pipeline
proceeds in three stages. It first crawls the web pages exposed by the
current environment,
$`\mathcal{D}^{(t)}=\textsc{Crawl}(\mathcal{E}^{(t)})`$, yielding a
corpus $`\mathcal{D}^{(t)}`$ of calendars, feeds, and developing news
from which questions can be posed. A generator then turns this corpus
into a set of candidate drafts,
$`\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}^{(t)}=\textsc{Gen}(\mathcal{D}^{(t)},\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}^{(t)})`$,
where each draft is a tuple of the form in Equation
([5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Prometheus: A Living Data Environment ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
and $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}^{(t)}`$ is the library of
task-synthesis skills that Athena feeds back to steer generation toward
Branchus’s weaknesses (Section
[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Athena: Recursive Evolution System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
A filter-and-select map finally yields the published batch, so that the
pipeline is the composition

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}=\textsc{Select}\circ\textsc{Filter}\big(\textsc{Gen}(\mathcal{D}^{(t)},\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}^{(t)})\big),
``` |  | (6) |

whose stages we now describe.

Validation and Temporal Filtering. The pipeline first identifies events
whose outcomes are expected to become observable within the requested
time horizon $`H`$, measured from the start of question generation. Once
the generation time $`t_{\mathrm{cut}}`$ is recorded, each candidate is
reassessed for temporal eligibility and is retained only if its deadline
and expected resolution time $`t_{\mathrm{res}}`$ satisfy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{\mathrm{cut}}\;<\;t_{\mathrm{dl}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad t_{\mathrm{cut}}\;<\;t_{\mathrm{res}}(q)\;\leq\;t_{\mathrm{cut}}+H,
``` |  | (7) |

so that the answer remains open at generation time and resolves within
the requested horizon.

Deduplication and Conflict Detection. The remaining drafts undergo
duplicate removal and conflict detection. Each draft receives a
reproducible identifier $`\mathrm{id}(q)`$ derived from the underlying
event $`e`$, the result $`o`$ being predicted, the answer format $`f`$,
and the relevant time boundaries. Drafts whose $`\mathrm{id}(q)`$
already appears in the question bank are excluded. Within the current
batch, drafts that share the same $`(e,o)`$ are compared: when their
structured attributes agree, one representative is retained despite
differences in wording; when they disagree, the group is discarded to
keep the published versions of a question consistent.

Diversity-Aware Selection. The remaining candidates are selected to
promote diversity across events, domains, sources, and question types.
The selector first favors events not yet represented in the batch. It
then considers a second question for an already represented event, up to
a maximum of two questions per event. Among otherwise comparable
candidates, it favors domains and sources with fewer questions in the
historical bank and current batch, followed by question types and answer
formats that occur less frequently in the current batch, and then
earlier forecast deadlines. This procedure promotes a diverse set of
questions, though the final distribution remains constrained by the
number of eligible questions available from each domain and source.

### 4.3 Branchus: Agentic Forecasting System

Branchus is the agentic forecaster that answers the questions posed by
Prometheus: given a question, it gathers evidence from the outside
world, reasons over it, and issues a probabilistic prediction, recording
the full trajectory that leads to each answer. Two mechanisms underpin
its design. A *multi-agent team* organization separates collecting
evidence from turning evidence into a prediction, so each part can be
scaled and improved independently. A *skill management* mechanism equips
the agents with an evolving repository of forecasting knowledge, from
hand-authored seeds to knowledge distilled from past experience.
Together these make Branchus both a strong forecaster and a producer of
the structured trajectories that Athena later learns from.

Multi-Agent Teams. Branchus factors the policy of Equation
([1](#S4.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
into two cooperating teams, a *search team*
$`\pi^{\mathrm{s}}_{\theta}`$ and a *predict team*
$`\pi^{\mathrm{p}}_{\theta}`$, organized by whether their work depends
on when it is done. The *search team* performs search: it collects and
vets evidence relevant to a question, and consists of a *searcher*, a
*scheduler*, and a *critic*. Its work is time-sensitive, because the
available evidence changes as an event approaches and, once the event
resolves, its answer becomes directly retrievable, so the same search
yields a different result depending on when it is run. The scheduler
decomposes the question and dispatches sub-agents, the searcher
retrieves information from external sources, and the critic assesses the
quality, relevance, and reliability of what has been gathered. The model
invokes these sub-agents on its own as needed, iterating between
retrieval and judgement until the evidence is sufficient, and every step
is retained as the search trajectory
$`\tau_{\mathrm{s}}\sim\pi^{\mathrm{s}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,\mathcal{S})`$.
The *predict team* performs prediction, turning this evidence into a
forecast. Its work is time-invariant, because it reasons only over
evidence already gathered: given the same evidence, it produces the same
forecast regardless of when it runs. Rather than re-searching, it calls
a local tool to access the search team’s cached reasoning trajectories,
which lets it aggregate a set $`\{\tau_{\mathrm{s}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{m}`$
of such trajectories into a single view of the evidence and reconcile
the partial conclusions they contain. From this aggregated evidence it
produces the final probabilistic answer,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{p}\;\sim\;\pi^{\mathrm{p}}_{\theta}\!\big(\,\cdot\mid q,\,\{\tau_{\mathrm{s}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{m},\,\mathcal{S}\,\big),
``` |  | (8) |

which recovers Equation
([1](#S4.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
with $`\tau=(\{\tau_{\mathrm{s}}^{(j)}\}_{j},\tau_{\mathrm{p}})`$. This
division of labour keeps evidence gathering and prediction loosely
coupled: the search team explores broadly and in parallel, while the
predict team concentrates the resulting trajectories into a calibrated
judgement.

Skill Management. Branchus draws on a repository of forecasting *skills*
$`\mathcal{S}`$, compact pieces of procedural knowledge that guide how a
question is approached. Skills are of two kinds. *Task-specific skills*
are authored by hand and form a seed set $`\mathcal{S}_{0}`$: each
encodes knowledge about a particular class of question, including
important source websites to consult and prompts that steer the
reasoning, giving the agent a useful starting competence before any
experience is accumulated. *Experience-distilled skills*, by contrast,
are consolidated from Branchus’s own trajectories by Athena and grow as
the system evolves, so that
$`\mathcal{S}^{(t)}=\mathcal{S}_{0}\cup\bigcup_{t^{\prime}<t}\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}(\mathcal{S}^{(t^{\prime})},\mathcal{T}^{(t^{\prime})})`$.
To make skills easy to organize, retrieve, and reuse, we structure each
skill as a four-level tuple $`s=(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3},s_{4})`$ ordered from
the abstract to the concrete, so that a general forecasting principle
$`s_{1}`$ at the top specializes progressively down to a concrete
procedure or source $`s_{4}`$ at the bottom. At inference time, an agent
assigned role $`a`$ to question $`q`$ retrieves a relevant subset and
keeps, for each matched skill, the most specific level that still
applies,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textsc{Retrieve}(q,a,\mathcal{S})\;=\;\big\{\,s_{\ell^{\star}(s)}:s\in\mathcal{S},\;\textsc{match}(s,q,a)\,\big\},\qquad\ell^{\star}(s)=\max\{\ell:s_{\ell}\text{ applies to }q\}.
``` |  | (9) |

This layered representation lets Branchus match a new question to skills
at the appropriate level of generality, so that a question without an
exact precedent still benefits from a broader level, and lets the
repository hold both broad heuristics and highly specific recipes within
a single consistent schema.

### 4.4 Athena: Recursive Evolution System

Athena is the recursive-evolution engine of EvoForesight: it extracts
experience from the trajectory pool $`\mathcal{T}^{(t)}`$ that Branchus
produces and turns it into improvement through the three operators of
Equation
([4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
At the parameter level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}`$ applies reinforcement
learning to Branchus’s predictions to update its weights $`\theta`$. At
the behaviour level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}`$ distils reusable skills
from its trajectories to strengthen the agent while leaving those
weights untouched. At the environment level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}`$
synthesizes adversarial skills from its failures to make Prometheus
generate harder, weakness-targeted tasks. The first two operators evolve
the agent and the third evolves the environment, so that both improve
from the same stream of experience.

Parameter-Level Evolution: Reinforcement Learning on Branchus’s
Predictions. At the parameter level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}`$ improves
Branchus by reinforcement learning, using Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) \[[23](#bib.bib8)\] on questions synthesized by
Prometheus. Training proceeds in two stages that separate evidence
gathering from parameter updates. First, the search team runs over these
questions and its reasoning trajectories $`\{\tau_{\mathrm{s}}\}`$ are
cached; once enough have accumulated, we perform reinforcement learning
with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on the predict team alone, using the
cached evidence. Training only the predict team on fixed, pre-collected
trajectories rules out answer leakage, since the model can no longer
shortcut the task by re-collecting evidence that trivially entails the
answer; yet because the evidence rather than the answer is fixed, the
predict team still explores freely, sampling $`G`$ candidate predictions
$`\{\hat{p}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ from the same evidence and updating on
their outcomes. Concretely, each sampled prediction receives the
verifiable reward of Equation
([2](#S4.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
$`r_{i}=r(q,\hat{p}_{i})\in\{0,1\}`$, which is turned into a
group-relative advantage by normalizing within the sampled group,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}\;=\;\frac{r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}\big(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)}{\mathrm{std}\big(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)},
``` |  | (10) |

and the predict team is updated by maximizing the clipped GRPO objective
over the fixed evidence,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}:\;\;\theta^{(t+1)}=\arg\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}^{(t)},\,\{\hat{p}_{i}\}\sim\pi^{\mathrm{p}}_{\theta^{(t)}}}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\min\!\Big(w_{i}(\theta)\,A_{i},\;\mathrm{clip}\big(w_{i}(\theta),1\!-\!\epsilon,1\!+\!\epsilon\big)A_{i}\Big)\right],
``` |  | (11) |

where
$`w_{i}(\theta)=\pi^{\mathrm{p}}_{\theta}(\hat{p}_{i}\mid q,\{\tau_{\mathrm{s}}^{(j)}\},\mathcal{S})/\pi^{\mathrm{p}}_{\theta^{(t)}}(\hat{p}_{i}\mid\cdot)`$
is the importance ratio and $`\epsilon`$ the clipping range. The
resolved ground truth $`y_{q}`$ from Prometheus supplies the reward
signal in Equation
([2](#S4.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
without human annotation. This regime motivated the multi-agent design:
by isolating prediction from search, the two-team organization makes it
possible to reinforce the predict team on cached evidence, so that the
measured improvement reflects better reasoning over the same information
rather than opportunistic re-collection.

Behavior-Level Evolution: Distilling Reusable Skills from Branchus’s
Trajectories. At the behavior level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}`$ turns
Branchus’s reasoning trajectories into reusable skills. These skills
guide the agent at inference time and improve how it works while leaving
its weights fixed. Formally, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}`$ maps the
trajectory pool to a set of new skills,
$`\Phi_{\mathrm{skill}}(\mathcal{S}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}^{(t)})=\mathcal{S}^{(t)}\cup\Delta\mathcal{S}^{(t)}`$,
through the composition
$`\Delta\mathcal{S}^{(t)}=(\textsc{Organize}\circ\textsc{Filter}\circ\textsc{Extract}\circ\textsc{Eval})(\mathcal{T}^{(t)})`$.
In the first stage, a judge model Eval scores the scheduler, searcher,
and critic of the search team against role-specific rubrics. The
resolved outcome $`y_{q}`$ is withheld from the judge, because forecast
correctness is an imperfect proxy for reasoning quality. In the second
stage, Extract uses these scores to identify positive experiences from
helpful but non-obvious actions, and negative experiences from recurring
mistakes or failure modes. Separating evaluation from extraction lets
each step focus on a single judgment. A Filter then discards weak
experiences. It removes those that merely restate a rubric, lack support
in the trajectory, or only prescribe which evidence to use rather than
how to forecast. In the third stage, Organize grades each surviving
experience into a four-level skill $`s=(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3},s_{4})`$: it
keeps the concrete procedure applied in the trajectory verbatim as the
most specific level $`s_{4}`$, and the three levels above it generalize
that procedure step by step, first to the question type, then within its
domain, and finally to a cross-domain principle $`s_{1}`$. Each level
stays within its role’s responsibility and remains independently
applicable, so the skill can be matched at whichever level of
abstraction fits a new question. At inference time an agent retrieves
skills by Equation
([9](#S4.E9 "Equation 9 ‣ 4.3 Branchus: Agentic Forecasting System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
so a question without an exact precedent still benefits from a broader
level. Because distillation needs no gradient update, $`\theta`$ stays
fixed and only $`\mathcal{S}`$ changes, in contrast to
$`\Phi_{\mathrm{rl}}`$. This makes distillation cheap enough to repeat
after every round.

Environment-Level Evolution: Adversarial Skill Synthesis Targeting
Branchus’s Weaknesses. At the environment level, $`\Phi_{\mathrm{env}}`$
turns feedback from past forecasts into task-synthesis skills
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}`$. These skills guide how Prometheus
generates later questions, which reshapes the environment
$`\mathcal{E}^{(t+1)}`$ and hence the next batch
$`\mathcal{Q}^{(t+1)}`$. They specify what types of questions to
construct and how to construct them, rather than how Branchus should
answer them. The goal is adversarial: expose categories of questions on
which Branchus has struggled, while keeping every task clear,
objectively verifiable, and reproducibly resolvable. The update starts
from the resolved triples $`\{(q,\hat{p},y_{q})\}`$ in
$`\mathcal{T}^{(t)}`$ and their rewards. We map each question to a
category $`c=\textsc{cat}(q)`$ by answer type and task feature, and
aggregate the evaluable predictions into an error profile

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{(t)}(c)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(q,\hat{p},y_{q}):\,\textsc{cat}(q)=c}\big[\,1-r(q,\hat{p})\,\big],
``` |  | (12) |

the mean error rate for category $`c`$. We read this profile as evidence
of category-level difficulty rather than as a direct diagnosis of a
reasoning failure, since a single error may simply reflect the intrinsic
uncertainty of an event. The profiled categories include numerical
forecasts, market prices, dynamic rankings, threshold judgments, and
high-variance events. The categories with the largest error,
$`\arg\max_{c}\rho^{(t)}(c)`$, mark where Branchus is least reliable,
and this signal directs where to construct new questions. Athena then
turns the signal into reusable construction guidance
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}^{(t)}=\textsc{Synthesize}(\rho^{(t)})`$.
Each synthesized skill specifies a target category, the conditions under
which it applies, how to discover relevant events, rules for building
questions, and quality constraints. These skills enter the generator, so
that Gen in $`\mathcal{E}^{(t+1)}`$ leans toward the identified
weaknesses. After the new questions are forecast and their outcomes
become available, we update the error profile of Equation
([12](#S4.E12 "Equation 12 ‣ 4.4 Athena: Recursive Evolution System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
and repeat the synthesis. This loop lets Prometheus adapt the task
distribution $`\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}`$ to Branchus’s observed weaknesses
across rounds, which keeps the recursion of Equation
([4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
from saturating.

### 4.5 Models and Implementation

Our evaluation pairs established agent harnesses with shared base LLMs
as strong external baselines, and adds in-framework comparisons that
isolate the core designs of EvoForesight. To make these comparisons
fair, we enforce implementation parity. Every harness runs on the same
Prometheus questions, receives the same external tools under identical
tool descriptions and a unified tool-calling format, and uses its own
official prompt. The only factors that vary across conditions are the
harness design and the base LLM. We avoid cross-paradigm comparisons
that would break this parity, such as static-corpus question answering
or dialogue, where evidence is already available rather than gathered
under uncertainty from an unfolding world. This keeps the gains reported
in Section
[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
attributable to the design of EvoForesight rather than to mismatched
task definitions. We now give the three concrete settings behind this
design.

Base LLMs and Agent Harnesses. We evaluate five representative frontier
LLMs that span different model families and capabilities: GPT-5.5,
GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude-Opus-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Qwen3.8-Max. This
range lets us test whether forecasting performance and evaluation
robustness hold across model families rather than for a single base
model. We pair each base LLM with six agent harnesses: ReAct, MAS,
OpenClaw, DeerFlow, MiroFlow, and Branchus, our purpose-built harness
for real-world event forecasting. These harnesses cover a broad range of
designs: a lightweight reasoning-and-tool-use loop (ReAct
\[[27](#bib.bib5)\]), a multi-agent system (MAS), and three
deep-research pipelines (OpenClaw \[[18](#bib.bib7)\], DeerFlow, and
MiroFlow), spanning general-purpose reasoning frameworks and
search-oriented systems. This model$`\times`$harness grid separates the
contribution of the base LLM from that of the harness, and shows how
harness design affects open-world forecasting across base models.

Prompt Specification. For each harness, we use its official prompt as
released by the original authors, rather than writing our own. This way,
every framework runs in the configuration it was designed and tuned for,
so performance differences reflect the harness design rather than our
prompt engineering. The complete prompt templates for the three modules
of EvoForesight are provided in Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting").

External Tool Settings. We give the models a web search tool that issues
queries and retrieves content, which grounds their forecasts in
up-to-date evidence. For Prometheus, we adopt the Codex
\[[17](#bib.bib4)\] harness and use its built-in tools to crawl news
from relevant web pages, which supplies the raw material for building
questions. We also design three local tools that expose the answer, the
reasoning trajectory, and the collected evidence of the search team to
the predict team of Branchus. With these tools, the predict team reuses
the search team’s outputs without issuing new external searches, so it
reasons over exactly the evidence already collected.

## Appendix A Full FutureX Overall Leaderboards

For completeness, we reproduce here the full official FutureX overall
leaderboards corresponding to the four weekly evaluations summarized in
Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting").
Each leaderboard reports the sliding-window Bradley–Terry rating of
every participating harness for the week in question, together with the
accompanying per-model statistics released by the benchmark. Whereas
Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Recursive evolution lifts EvoForesight to the strongest forecasting system ‣ 2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
retains only the harnesses relevant to our comparison, the tables below
list the complete field of entrants, allowing the position of Branchus
to be read against the entire leaderboard rather than the reduced set.
Across the first three weeks Branchus attains the top overall rating; in
the final week it remains among the strongest entrants, and we discuss
the factors behind this week-to-week variation in Section
[2](#S2 "2 Results ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting").

![Refer to

## Appendix B Real World Event Forecasting

### B.1 2026 Nobel Prize

To test our system on high-stakes, real-world events, we applied
Branchus to forecasting the 2026 Nobel Prizes. This task carries genuine
uncertainty, no training-set leakage, and a hard public resolution date.
To make the evaluation fully pre-registered and verifiable, we published
each forecast on X *before* the corresponding laureates were announced.
Table
[3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ B.1 2026 Nobel Prize ‣ Appendix B Real World Event Forecasting ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
lists the five posts, one per prize. These timestamped, publicly
committed predictions rule out hindsight and let any reader audit
exactly what the system claimed, and when, against the subsequent
announcements.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Prize | Published forecast |
| Physics | [x.com/BranchusAI/status/2107395342539030965](https://x.com/BranchusAI/status/2107395342539030965) |
| Chemistry | [x.com/BranchusAI/status/2107756760409034917](https://x.com/BranchusAI/status/2107756760409034917) |
| Literature | [x.com/BranchusAI/status/2108101909391524193](https://x.com/BranchusAI/status/2108101909391524193) |
| Peace | [x.com/BranchusAI/status/2108460181793419444](https://x.com/BranchusAI/status/2108460181793419444) |
| Economics | [x.com/BranchusAI/status/2109501869265658231](https://x.com/BranchusAI/status/2109501869265658231) |

Table 3: Pre-announcement forecasts for the 2026 Nobel Prizes, published
on X before each laureate was announced.

The 2026 Nobel Prizes are among the hardest forecasting targets
imaginable. Each prize draws from a pool of thousands of plausible
nominees, the committee’s deliberations are sealed for fifty years, and
the final choice frequently rewards an outsider rather than the
consensus front-runner. No historical pattern or odds board reliably
anticipates the outcome, and the field of candidates any single
forecaster can realistically track is a vanishing fraction of the true
pool. A correct call therefore cannot be reverse-engineered from
training data or market odds; it demands genuinely original
evidence-gathering about who is in contention and why.

This difficulty defeats even the strongest systems. Fig.
[12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.1 2026 Nobel Prize ‣ Appendix B Real World Event Forecasting ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
compares the pre-announcement forecasts on the two prizes with the most
extreme outsiders. The first is the Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded to
Francis Halzen “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino
Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical
origin.” The second is the Nobel Peace Prize, awarded to Navi Pillay
“for her efforts to promote peace and international law.” In both cases
the eventual laureate was an outsider that essentially no forecaster
took seriously: frontier agent systems, standalone web-search models
backed by the most capable LLMs, and the Kalshi prediction market alike
assigned the candidate no meaningful probability. None of them even
listed the laureate, and none beat the trivial no-forecast baseline. Raw
model strength, in other words, was not enough.

Yet our system succeeded where they all failed. Branchus was the sole
forecaster to surface and list either laureate, namely Halzen in Physics
and Pillay in Peace, doing so in one of its three independent runs.
Where every competitor left both laureates entirely off its slate, our
system put them on the board. This ability to unearth a credible but
overlooked candidate, rather than merely echoing consensus
front-runners, reflects the broader and more exhaustive evidence that
Branchus gathers before committing to a forecast.

![Refer to caption](2610.29784v2/figures/NobelPrize/PhysicsRank.jpeg)

Beyond the two outsider prizes above, the Literature and Economics
prizes test forecasting on more consensus-driven fields where many
forecasters cluster on the same front-runners. Fig.

shows, for each prize, the per-candidate probability every forecaster
assigned before the announcement. The two prizes probe complementary
behaviours. (1) *Literature.* Here our advantage is one of reliability.
Although several forecasters placed mass on the eventual laureate, Anne
Carson, only Branchus, OpenClaw, and GPT-6 Pro ranked her first in any
run, and Branchus’s other two runs both ranked her second. Every single
one of our runs therefore placed the eventual laureate in the top two, a
level of stability no competitor matched. Taken together with Peace,
where Branchus alone surfaced the laureate, our system ranks the true
winner in its top two across both prizes, a consistency that
distinguishes a system that genuinely reasons about the field from one
that happens to guess right once. (2) *Economics.* The 2026 prize was
shared, but no forecaster, ours included, listed both laureates; every
run surfaced only one of the two winners. On the finer-grained
probability assigned to the laureate it did list, Branchus lands in the
middle of the field, neither notably strong nor weak relative to the
other systems, consistent with a shared prize whose second recipient
none of the forecasters anticipated.

## Appendix C Evaluation Metrics

This appendix specifies, in full, the metrics used to score the
Prometheus-synthesized evaluation. Our goal is to characterize a
forecaster along three complementary axes—how often it is right, how
trustworthy its stated probabilities are, and how much compute it
spends—rather than to collapse everything onto a single number. We write
$`\mathcal{I}`$ for the set of scored harness–LLM systems, index its
members by $`i`$, and set $`M=|\mathcal{I}|`$. Questions come in two
families, which we handle separately: a *choice* track and a *numeric*
track, denoted by the superscript $`t\in\{c,n\}`$. The question set of a
track is $`\mathcal{Q}^{t}`$ and its cardinality is
$`N^{t}=|\mathcal{Q}^{t}|`$.

### C.1 Choice Forecasts

Consider a single-answer choice question $`q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}`$
offering $`K_{q}`$ options, with resolved option $`y_{q}`$. System $`i`$
emits a probability $`p_{iqk}`$ for each option $`k`$. From this vector
we read off the option the system would commit to, the probability it
places on that option, and whether the commitment was right:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{y}_{iq}`$ | $`\displaystyle\in\arg\max_{k}p_{iqk},`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle c_{iq}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\max_{k}p_{iqk},`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{iq}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{\hat{y}_{iq}=y_{q}\}.`$ |  |

Accuracy and Brier score. Accuracy is simply the share of questions
whose top-probability option turns out to be the resolved one,

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{Acc}_{i}=\frac{1}{N^{c}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}a_{iq},
       ```                                                                |     |

and we report it as a percentage. Accuracy throws away the magnitude of
a forecast, so we pair it with the Brier score, which rewards a system
for placing mass on the correct option and penalizes mass placed
elsewhere. For one question this is the squared distance between the
predicted probability vector and the one-hot resolution,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{BS}_{iq}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{q}}\left(p_{iqk}-\mathbf{1}\{k=y_{q}\}\right)^{2},
``` |  |

and the reported figure averages it over the track,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Brier}_{i}=\frac{1}{N^{c}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}\mathrm{BS}_{iq}.
``` |  |

We keep the full sum over options rather than dividing by $`K_{q}`$.
Higher accuracy and lower Brier are better.

Negative log-likelihood and its tail. The negative log-likelihood looks
only at the probability assigned to the option that actually resolved,
and so punishes a confident mistake far more sharply than Brier does.
Per question and in aggregate,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{iq}=-\ln p_{iq,y_{q}},\qquad\mathrm{NLL}_{i}=\frac{1}{N^{c}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}\ell_{iq}.
``` |  |

Because the mean can hide catastrophic single-question losses, we
additionally report a tail statistic that averages only the
$`h=\lceil 0.1N^{c}\rceil`$ worst cases,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{TailNLL}_{i}=\frac{1}{h}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{W}_{i}}\ell_{iq},
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{W}_{i}`$ collects the $`h`$ highest-loss questions for
system $`i`$. Logarithms are natural throughout, so these quantities are
in nats, and smaller is better on both.

Confidence gap. A useful forecaster should be more confident when it is
right than when it is wrong. We therefore split mean confidence by
outcome,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle C_{i}^{+}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}a_{iq}c_{iq}}{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}a_{iq}},\qquad C_{i}^{-}=\frac{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}(1-a_{iq})c_{iq}}{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{c}}(1-a_{iq})},`$ |  |

report the confidence-when-wrong term as $`100C_{i}^{-}`$ percent, and
define the confidence gap as the difference $`100(C_{i}^{+}-C_{i}^{-})`$
in percentage points. A wide gap says the stated confidence carries real
information about correctness; a gap near zero says it does not.

AUROC. We summarize the same discrimination with a threshold-free
quantity: treating a correct answer as the positive class and the
forecaster’s confidence as the ranking score, the area under the ROC
curve is the probability that a randomly drawn correct answer was more
confident than a randomly drawn incorrect one,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{AUROC}_{i}=\Pr(c_{i}^{+}>c_{i}^{-})+\frac{1}{2}\Pr(c_{i}^{+}=c_{i}^{-}),
``` |  |

with the probabilities taken as empirical frequencies over all
correct–incorrect pairs and ties split evenly. Values closer to one mean
the confidence ranking separates right from wrong more cleanly.

Expected calibration error. Confidence should also match realized
frequency in an absolute sense. We bin predictions into the ten
equal-width confidence intervals $`[0,0.1),\ldots,[0.9,1]`$, write
$`n_{ib}`$ for the count in bin $`b`$ and
$`\mathrm{acc}_{ib},\mathrm{conf}_{ib}`$ for the mean correctness and
mean confidence there, and take the count-weighted discrepancy between
the two,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{ECE}_{i}=\sum_{b=1}^{10}\frac{n_{ib}}{N^{c}}\left|\mathrm{acc}_{ib}-\mathrm{conf}_{ib}\right|.
``` |  |

Empty bins drop out of the sum. A lower ECE means stated confidence
tracks empirical accuracy more faithfully.

### C.2 Numeric Forecasts

A numeric question $`q\in\mathcal{Q}^{n}`$ resolves to a scalar
$`y_{q}`$. System $`i`$ reports a mean $`\mu_{iq}`$ together with a set
of predictive quantiles $`v_{iq,\tau}`$.

Weighted interval score. The seven elicited quantiles pin down a
predictive median $`m_{iq}=v_{iq,0.50}`$ and the central $`50\%`$,
$`80\%`$, and $`90\%`$ intervals. For each nominal miscoverage
$`\alpha\in\mathcal{A}=\{0.10,0.20,0.50\}`$ the interval runs from
$`l_{iq,\alpha}=v_{iq,\alpha/2}`$ to
$`u_{iq,\alpha}=v_{iq,1-\alpha/2}`$, and its interval score charges for
the width of the interval plus a penalty, scaled by $`2/\alpha`$,
whenever the outcome falls outside it:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{IS}_{iq,\alpha}=u_{iq,\alpha}-l_{iq,\alpha}+\frac{2}{\alpha}(l_{iq,\alpha}-y_{q})_{+}+\frac{2}{\alpha}(y_{q}-u_{iq,\alpha})_{+},
``` |  |

with $`(x)_{+}=\max(x,0)`$. The weighted interval score blends these
with the absolute median error,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{WIS}_{iq}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|y_{q}-m_{iq}|+\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\alpha}{2}\mathrm{IS}_{iq,\alpha}}{3.5},
``` |  |

and so rewards intervals that are both tight and well placed. It is
reported in the target’s own units; we form cross-target rankings only
through within-question comparisons, never by averaging raw WIS across
targets. Lower is better.

Median symmetric absolute percentage error. For point accuracy we use
the predicted mean and a scale-free, symmetric error,

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{sAPE}_{iq}=200\frac{|\mu_{iq}-y_{q}|}{|\mu_{iq}|+|y_{q}|},
       ```                                                                 |     |

set to zero when $`\mu_{iq}=y_{q}=0`$. Taking the median across
questions avoids letting a handful of large-magnitude targets dominate,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Md\text{-}sAPE}_{i}=\operatorname{median}_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{n}}\mathrm{sAPE}_{iq}.
``` |  |

It is a percentage, and smaller values mean tighter point forecasts.

### C.3 Relative Comparisons

Because scores on different tracks live on different scales, our
head-to-head comparisons are built from per-question wins rather than
averaged losses. On a given question we compare systems $`i`$ and $`j`$
using Brier for choice questions and WIS for numeric questions, with
lower loss winning. The outcome $`w_{ijq}`$ is one for a win, one-half
for a tie, and zero for a loss; ties are detected first, using a
relative tolerance of $`10^{-10}`$ and no absolute tolerance.

WIS win rate. On the numeric track we average these outcomes over all
questions and all opponents,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{WinRate}_{i}=\frac{100}{N^{n}(M-1)}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{n}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in\mathcal{I}\\
j\neq i\end{subarray}}w_{ijq},
``` |  |

so that every question and opponent counts equally and a tie is worth
half a win. Higher is better.

Bradley–Terry scores. To fold both tracks into one rating we first
aggregate pairwise outcomes per track, letting each question carry total
weight one spread across its $`\binom{M}{2}`$ unordered pairs,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
W_{ij}^{t}=\frac{1}{\binom{M}{2}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{t}}w_{ijq},
``` |  |

and then combine the tracks so that choice and numeric forecasting
contribute equally,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
W_{ij}^{\mathrm{joint}}=\frac{W_{ij}^{c}}{2N^{c}}+\frac{W_{ij}^{n}}{2N^{n}}.
``` |  |

We fit the Bradley–Terry model \[[3](#bib.bib28)\], in which the odds of
$`i`$ beating $`j`$ depend on a latent strength difference,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr(i\succ j)=\sigma(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j}),\qquad\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}},
``` |  |

by weighted maximum likelihood under a zero-sum constraint,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\theta}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\sum_{i}\theta_{i}=0}\sum_{i\neq j}W_{ij}^{\mathrm{joint}}\ln\sigma(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j}).
``` |  |

The headline score is $`100\sigma(\hat{\theta}_{i})`$, the fitted win
probability against a neutral opponent at $`\theta=0`$; higher means
stronger. Stratum-level ratings are refit from scratch on the relevant
track and stratum, each with its own zero-sum constraint, and are
therefore not directly comparable across strata.

### C.4 Stratified Diagnostics

Aggregate scores average over questions of very different hardness, so
we also slice the evaluation along two axes that are computed from the
forecasts themselves and never from the resolution. *Difficulty*
captures how uncertain the consensus forecast is, and *disagreement*
captures how much the systems diverge from one another. Each axis is cut
into three tiers at its empirical $`1/3`$ and $`2/3`$ quantiles within
the track, with boundary values assigned to the lower tier.

Difficulty and disagreement. For a choice question we average the
probability vectors across systems, renormalize to a distribution, and
take its normalized entropy,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
U_{q}^{c}=-\frac{1}{\ln K_{q}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{q}}\bar{p}_{qk}\ln\bar{p}_{qk},\qquad 0\ln 0=0,
``` |  |

so a confident consensus scores near zero and a diffuse one near one.
For a numeric question we take the median across systems of the
symmetric relative width of the $`90\%`$ interval,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
U_{q}^{n}=\operatorname{median}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{2(v_{iq,0.95}-v_{iq,0.05})}{|v_{iq,0.95}|+|v_{iq,0.05}|},
``` |  |

treating a zero denominator as zero width. Choice disagreement is the
option-summed variance of the predicted probabilities, rescaled so
questions with different option counts are comparable,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{q}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{q}}\operatorname{Var}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}(p_{iqk})}{1-1/K_{q}},
``` |  |

with the variance taken in the population sense (divisor $`M`$).
Difficulty gives Easy/Medium/Hard tiers and disagreement gives
Low/Medium/High tiers.

Absolute and question-adjusted losses. Inside a stratum we report both
an absolute level of error—mean Brier for choice questions, median
$`100\,\mathrm{WIS}_{iq}/|y_{q}|`$ for numeric questions—and a
question-adjusted version that removes the effect of which questions
each system happened to answer. For choice questions we subtract the
per-question mean Brier,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\mathrm{BS}_{iq}=\mathrm{BS}_{iq}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\mathrm{BS}_{jq},
``` |  |

and for numeric questions we use the log ratio of WIS to the question’s
geometric-mean WIS,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{iq}=\ln\widetilde{\mathrm{WIS}}_{iq}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\ln\widetilde{\mathrm{WIS}}_{jq}.
``` |  |

For the logarithm we replace a zero WIS by half the smallest positive
WIS on the same question, or set the adjusted value to zero if every WIS
there is zero; the pairwise win comparisons above still use the
untouched WIS values. A negative adjusted loss means the system beats
the question-level reference. These adjusted scores are averaged over
the questions in each stratum, harness-level summaries take the
arithmetic mean across base models, and normalized Brier differences
divide each per-question score by $`1-1/K_{q}`$, the Brier score of the
uniform forecast.

## Appendix D Prompt Templates

For completeness and reproducibility, this section collects the core
prompt templates that drive the three modules of EvoForesight. We
present them in the order in which they participate in one round of the
recursive self-improvement loop (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.1 Overview ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")):
first the prompt with which Prometheus synthesizes forecasting questions
(Appendix
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Prometheus: Question Synthesis Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"));
then the prompt with which Branchus gathers evidence and issues a
probabilistic prediction (Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Branchus: Forecasting Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"));
then the two prompts through which Athena learns from the resulting
trajectories, namely the judge prompt that evaluates each trajectory
(Appendix
[D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Athena: Action-level evaluation prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"))
and the prompt that distils reusable skills from it (Appendix
[D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Athena: Skill Extraction Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting"));
and finally the prompt with which Athena synthesizes adversarial
task-construction skills that drive environment-level evolution
(Appendix
[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Athena: Environment-Level Skill Synthesis Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Placeholders of the form {{…}} are filled in at runtime with the
relevant question, trajectory, evidence, or skill content. The templates
below are lightly edited for presentation; the full runtime versions
include additional formatting instructions and output schemas that we
omit here for brevity.

### D.1 Prometheus: Question Synthesis Prompt

Prometheus uses the prompt in Prompt
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Prometheus: Question Synthesis Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
to turn crawled web content into candidate forecasting questions that
are objective, short-horizon, and reproducibly resolvable, each
structured as the tuple $`q=(e,o,f,t_{\mathrm{cut}},t_{\mathrm{dl}})`$
of Equation
([5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Prometheus: A Living Data Environment ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
The prompt directs the model to read and operate the
prediction-question-factory skill; Prompt
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Prometheus: Question Synthesis Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
reproduces that skill’s specification (its skill document SKILL.md),
which defines the construction CLI, build semantics, and the boundary of
what may be published. When Athena has produced task-synthesis skills
$`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{env}}`$ (Appendix
[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Athena: Environment-Level Skill Synthesis Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
they are additionally injected into the {{synthesis_skills}} field to
steer generation toward Branchus’s weaknesses. We abridge the
question-synthesis prompt for presentation, keeping the operative
instructions and dropping the full output schema and reporting
checklist.

### D.2 Branchus: Forecasting Prompt

Branchus factors forecasting into a search team and a predict team
(Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Branchus: Agentic Forecasting System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")).
Prompt
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Branchus: Forecasting Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")
drives the search team’s evidence gathering and Prompt

drives the predict team’s probabilistic judgement over the aggregated
evidence. Both are conditioned on the retrieved skill subset
$`\textsc{Retrieve}(q,a,\mathcal{S})`$ of Equation
([9](#S4.E9 "Equation 9 ‣ 4.3 Branchus: Agentic Forecasting System ‣ 4 Approach ‣ Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting")),
injected into the {{skills}} field.
````
